companies like microsoft and social media companies like Meta on a wide range of initiatives,
from digital literacy and training programs that help strengthen the information ecosystem to
[insert Meta health or other program here], that support development goals. Like other private
sector partnerships, programming and partnerships with tech companies and social media
companies is common and continues to be encouraged. That has not changed. That is business
as usual. This guidance also is not about General use of USAID's social media is not restricted.

What has changed is an increase in information manipulation, such as x, in particular by foreign
malign influence or non-state actors. More information manipulation is occurring on social media
platforms. It has impacted USAID's work and its partners. In a subset of cases like [doxxing or
otherwise harmful content] social media platforms. This has prompted more interest at USAID
and within the USG in engaging social media companies and tech companies about ways to
combat it. Under certain circumstances this engagement might include content moderation
requests.
This is where the GC guidance fits into the larger IIR guidance. It is focused on providing
guardrails for communications with social media companies that could touch on content
moderation because they trigger legal concerns about the first amendment, freedom of
expression, and the privacy act. Content moderation is an area of heightened legal risk as
evidenced by recent Supreme Court litigation, heightened reputational risk, and high levels of
congressional scrutiny and oversight.
A. USAID's longstanding commitment to protecting and promoting freedom of expression,
and free and independent media consistent with the United States' responsibilities as a
party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which protects freedom
of expression, and the right to freedom of speech protected by the First Amendment to
the United States Constitution. In the United States, freedom of expression - whether
exercised offline or online - receives strong protection. The First Amendment to the U.S
Constitution states that "Congress shall make no law ... abridging the freedom of
speech." The United States Supreme Court has interpreted the right to freedom of
speech broadly and has only identified a limited number of narrowly defined categories
of speech that do not receive First Amendment protection.

Topline Guidance for Communications with Social Media Platforms
Topline GC guidance: If the conversation veers toward discussions about having specific posts
or content removed, retained, posted, or promoted, USAID should redirect the conversation. If
possible, stick to flagging general issues or trends or discussion of what the platform and USAID
are doing programmatically or via policy to address those issues or trends and redirect or table
anything that is potentially a landmine or complicated.

Thank you for your patience. My understanding from your email is that Meta sent an email to
your leadership, Marcela Escobari and Mileydi Guilarte, requesting that they meet with Meta's
Public Policy Director for Meta in Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean while he is in DC
in early April to provide an overview of their key workstreams, including an update on Meta
initiatives in the region, how they are addressing the root cause of migration, and election
integrity. I think it would be fine for USAID to take this meeting.
I would recommend a couple general guardrails: Prep talking points or a briefer. If no such
documents are prepared I recommend flagging one key landmine for your principals. If the
conversation veers toward discussions about having specific posts or content removed,
retained, posted, or promoted, redirect. If possible, stick to flagging general issues or trends or
discussion of what Meta and USAID are doing programmatically or via policy to address those

issues or trends and redirect or table anything that is potentially a landmine or complicated
The applicable FAQ from the Guidance is O#16
Some additional detail regarding the guardrails included below.
• Given the sensitivities in this space, the fact that Meta is setting the agenda, and the
fact that this discussion is taking place at the leadership rather than working level, I
recommend that USAID be in listening mode where possible, avoid making any firm
commitments and that any action items or next steps be determined at a fairly high
level so there is an opportunity for USAID SMEs to review and discuss first.
• Talk about general issue areas/pain points or trends is ok (e.g., "Meta has noticed
there is a rise in threats against politicians, especially women, in country x during
election time. Meta did x in the past and is planning to do y in the future. If USAID has
expertise it can share on country conditions and trends on these issues it would be
helpful.").
•
if your leadership prefers for concrete deliverables/decisions to come out of the
meeting, then I strongly recommend additional prep on the front end, such as talking
points or briefers.
• Redirect or table any conversations about specific content moderation requests (e.g.,
"Group x posted inflammatory language. What does USAID think should be done
about it?").
• If talking points, briefers or other prep documents will be prepared for the principals
in advance of this meeting I recommend sharing them with GC and RLO for awareness
and a quick check for any potential landmines.

Other summary
On Friday, September 8, 2023, the Fifth Circuit issued an order significantly narrowing the
scope of the preliminary injunction in Missouri v. Biden.
As a result, USAID is no longer prohibited from engaging in activities touching on content
moderation in concert with State.
The Fifth Circuit found the injunction to be vague and overbroad, vacated the majority of it,
narrowed it to apply only to the White House, the Surgeon General, CDC, and FBI and excluded
all other parties, including the State Department. The Fifth Circuit determined certain White
House, CDC and FBI officials' content moderation activities regarding COVID-19 disinformation
might have violated the First Amendment, but did not find sufficient evidence that the other
named defendants were likely to have done so.
Talking points for the committee folks
CONTENT MODERATION
Background: On July 4, 2024, a federal district court in Louisiana issued a preliminary
injunction in Missouri v. Biden prohibiting the State Department, several other federal agencies,
White House officials and anyone acting "in concert" with them from directly or indirectly
(through third parties or implementing partners) urging or pressuring social media companies to
remove or suppress "protected free speech." The injunction identified a few exceptions to this
USAID was not named in the injunction, but its activities were impacted in certain
circumstances, such as when USAID collaborated on activities with the State Department or

other federal agencies named in the injunction. State issued guidance regarding content
moderation activities. USAID was prohibited from engaging in content moderation activities in
concert with State or other parties named in the injunction. OUs were instructed to consult GC
for guidance.
On July 14, 2023, the Fifth Circuit granted a temporary administrative stay of the preliminary
injunction previously issued in the case of Missouri v. Biden. The stay remains in place pending
further orders from the court. Oral arguments were heard on August 10, 2023. GC is closely
monitoring the status of this case and will inform DRG of any changes. As a result of the stay,
DRG can resume activities that involve engagement with social media companies and can
coordinate with State on such matters, with some guardrails.
In short, USAID should continue to exercise appropriate caution in how it engages with tech
companies. Put your FOIA+ or litigation lens on.
More detail on the guardrails is provided below:
• Avoid "content moderation" - My understanding is that DRG does not anticipate
flagging to social media companies content for removal or increased scrutiny or
attention ( (e.g., posts by certain individuals or entities), but if it does occur, DRG
should only do it in the most limited and exceptional circumstances, and only in close
• Avoid or exercise significant caution regarding any discussions with social
media companies of their "content moderation" policies - Similarly, If DRG will be
reaching out to any social media companies to discuss their policies or approaches to
content moderation (e.g., encourage them to strengthen safeguards), please touch
base with GC prior to outreach. Cleared talking points are recommended.
Maximize use of cleared talking points for DRG led meetings -lf DRG will be
hosting meetings involving discussions with social media companies that might
directly or indirectly touch on content moderation, GC recommends preparing
agendas and talking points and clearing them with GC.
• Coordination - Confirm (if possible) that State L has cleared on/is aware of any
State-led joint State/USAID engagements with social media companies involving
discussions of "content moderation" - Talking points cleared by GC are
recommended. GC should also be consulted on any planned strategies to promote or
amplify any frameworks or documents to help reduce the risk that such efforts are
misconstrued as coercive. USAID should exercise additional caution in re-engaging
with State on any initiative involving "content moderation" which lacks a written
roadmap or overview for social media company engagement, cleared talking points, or
clearance/socialization with State L.

HYGIENE
• Only write things that pass the Washington Post Test
• Be thoughtful about word choice. Gossip, angry comments, profanity, and other
unprofessional statements generally WILL be disclosed.
• The fact that the release of a record would be personally embarrassing is not grounds to
not disclose.
• Do not write,
"this is too sensitive to discuss over email," "this is highly sensitive, we
shouldn't put any of this in writing" or "not to be shared further." Think about the word
choice. Is there another word you can use? (e.g., peer competitor)
• If in doubt, pick up the phone.
• Less than gracious comments about other components of USAID or the USG are good
fodder for fire
• Keep emails professional and courteous.
• Be precise about language. Avoid language that might raise red flags (e.g., influence,
change, shape)
• Terminology - peer competitors (coordinate with LPA)
